title: Texas Governor Greg Abbott Freezes H-1B Hiring Across State Agencies, Universities and Public Schools
excerpt: The executive order blocks new H-1B visa petitions at taxpayer-funded institutions until May 2027, adding Texas to a growing list of states restricting skilled foreign worker hiring.
body:
• Governor Greg Abbott has ordered a freeze on all new H-1B visa petitions at Texas state agencies, public universities and school districts, effective immediately through May 31, 2027.
  • Any agency seeking an exception must obtain written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, creating a de facto ban on foreign skilled worker hiring with taxpayer funds.
  • Indians hold roughly 71% of all H-1B approvals in the United States, making them disproportionately affected by any state-level restrictions on the visa program.
  • Major research institutions including UT Southwestern Medical Center and MD Anderson Cancer Center could face recruitment challenges for specialized roles.

Abbott's Executive Order Targets Taxpayer-Funded Employers

Texas Governor Greg Abbott signed an executive order on Monday freezing all new H-1B visa petitions filed by state agencies, public universities and school districts until May 31, 2027. The directive requires any state entity seeking to sponsor a foreign worker to first obtain written permission from the Texas Workforce Commission, effectively creating a gatekeeper for every H-1B filing that uses public funds.

"State government must lead by example and ensure that employment opportunities — particularly those funded with taxpayer dollars — are filled by Texans first," Abbott said in a statement accompanying the order.

"State government must lead by example and ensure that employment opportunities — particularly those funded with taxpayer dollars — are filled by Texans first."

— Greg Abbott, Governor of Texas

The order does not affect private-sector employers, who account for the vast majority of H-1B sponsorships in the state. Technology firms, oil and gas companies, and healthcare systems operating outside the public university network remain free to file petitions without state interference.

Research Institutions Face Recruitment Squeeze

Texas is home to some of the nation's most prominent medical and research institutions that rely heavily on international talent. UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and the broader University of Texas system employ thousands of H-1B workers in roles ranging from biomedical researchers to specialized physicians.

Higher education administrators have privately expressed concern that the freeze could hamper their ability to attract top-tier researchers, particularly in STEM fields where competition for talent is fierce. International scholars often serve as principal investigators on federally funded grants, and delays in hiring could ripple through ongoing research programs.

Public school districts, which employ foreign-born teachers in shortage areas like bilingual education and special education, are also covered by the order. Several Texas districts have historically used H-1B visas to fill positions where qualified American candidates are scarce.

A Growing State-Level Trend

Texas joins Florida in imposing state-level restrictions on H-1B hiring within government and public institutions. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis signed a similar executive order in 2023, directing state agencies to prioritize domestic hiring. Several other Republican-led states have introduced legislative proposals along the same lines, though few have enacted binding restrictions.

The orders reflect a broader political current within the Republican Party that has increasingly framed the H-1B program as displacing American workers, despite the visa's original design as a tool for filling positions requiring specialized knowledge that domestic labor markets cannot supply.

Disproportionate Impact on Indian Professionals

Indians are by far the largest group of H-1B recipients, accounting for approximately 71% of all approvals. The visa has long served as the primary pathway for Indian engineers, scientists and medical professionals to build careers in the United States, and any contraction of the program — even at the state level — sends a signal that reverberates through recruitment pipelines back in India.

"The freeze creates an environment of uncertainty for international researchers who may look to institutions in other states — or other countries — that are still actively competing for talent."

— Bloomberg Law analysis

For Indian professionals already employed at Texas public institutions on H-1B visas, the executive order does not affect existing sponsorships. The freeze applies only to new petitions, though it could complicate renewals and transfers within the public sector if the TWC adopts a restrictive interpretation of its gatekeeping role.

What Comes Next

The order is set to remain in effect through May 31, 2027, though Abbott could extend or modify it. Legal challenges are possible — immigration attorneys have noted that state-level interference with a federally administered visa program could face constitutional scrutiny under the Supremacy Clause. However, because the order restricts state agencies' own hiring decisions rather than directly regulating the visa program, its legal footing may be more secure than a broader prohibition would be.

The Texas Workforce Commission has not yet issued guidance on how it will process exception requests, leaving public institutions in limbo as the fall hiring season approaches.
